reference_opening.argument: This video is scam content because it promotes deploying a front-running bot, asks viewers to fund its contract with approximately 0.5 to 2 BNB, and claims the transfer can generate thousands per day while returning 90 percent of stated profits to the wallet. The speaker demonstrates deploying the contract and sending roughly 0.5 to 1 BNB, then describes automated trades and potential daily gains of up to 100 BNB with more capital. The video acknowledges that fees may consume deposited money, and the described material does not establish that the contract functions as claimed or that the displayed transaction produced profit.

you just follow the description of the video as far as downloading metamask and also funding it
the next step in this process is just funding your contract
for the sake of this video I'm just going to do 0.5 bnb – actually might just make it 1, a bit extra
then it engages all the constructors that are built in as far as engaging the pancake router. It automatically buys and sells for you

opening.argument: Judge, the funding guidance includes an explicit warning that the contract can consume money in fees, not just produce returns: the description says it could “waste your money on fees” and warns “you may lose capital.” The speaker also acknowledges paying gas during deployment. These cautions matter when assessing whether the video presents funding as a risk-free way to get paid. Its profit claims may be ambitious, but the viewer is told that costs can defeat the proposed strategy.

citations.quote: the contract will basically waste your money on fees rather than use it to make a profit.
you may lose capital.
there we go we paid a little gas that should be fine

rebuttal.rebuttal: The opening points to funding instructions and claimed returns, but those facts do not make the pitch unqualified. The omitted warning says that insufficient funding could leave the contract spending money on fees rather than profit. The speaker's demonstrated transfer is also described as funding “the contract we just created,” which leaves open the reading that this is a risky user-deployed trading experiment rather than a payment to the presenter.

citations.quote: If you fund the contract with less than 0.5 BNB, the bot might target another token with high burn fees the contract will basically waste your money on fees rather than use it to make a profit.
we're just going to send some funds to that contract we just created

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The warning is real, but it frames loss chiefly as a consequence of funding too little, then recommends putting more BNB into the contract. It does not substantiate the bot's returns. The same description promises passive earnings of thousands a day, while the speaker instructs viewers to fund and activate the contract. Disclosing a fee risk does not resolve the unsupported profit pitch tied to a requested transfer.

citations.quote: I recommend funding the contract with around 0.5 - 2 BNB just to make sure that won't happen.
you will be able to passively generate thousands a day
After it's sent to the contract contract we'll just go over here and press the action button.

opening.argument: Judge, much of the recording is a hands-on contract walkthrough. The speaker tells viewers how to create a file in Remix, copy contract information, select a Solidity compiler version, connect a wallet and check the deployed address on BSC Scan. The sampled frames likewise show a code editor, deployment controls and a contract page. Those concrete steps support reading the video as an operational demonstration. The speaker's asserted results should not be mistaken for independently verified performance, but their presence does not erase the instructional substance of what is shown.

citations.quote: I'm going to go into contracts under contracts. I'm going to create a new contract which is with this new file.
we're going to copy the contract information that I put in the description
I paste it in BSC Scan. We can see that it's in the address there now.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The opening correctly notes the deployment, funding and claimed automated trades. But a demonstration of those steps does not, by itself, prove a fraudulent transfer or establish that the speaker controls the destination contract. The speaker says the address being funded belongs to the contract just created, and the sampled wallet frame shows a transaction being prepared. Those details support evaluating this as a tutorial with unverified claims, rather than treating the mechanics of deployment as proof of deception.

citations.quote: we're just going to send some funds to that contract we just created

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The technical walkthrough is also the means by which viewers are directed to fund and activate the proposed bot. The description supplies contract code to copy, tells viewers to run it, and promises passive earnings. Neither a code editor nor a contract listing verifies that the code performs the claimed trades or sends profits back. Instructional detail does not neutralize a funded-contract pitch built around extraordinary, unverified returns.

you will be able to passively generate thousands a day
The front run bot will transfer the profit back to your wallet.

opening.argument: Judge, the proposed activity is described as trading through a deployed contract: funds enter a “Frontrun Pool,” the bot is said to buy and sell, and proceeds are said to return to the viewer's wallet. The cited instructions do ask for capital, but they do not show a purchase from the presenter, a recruitment requirement or a request for wallet credentials. The speaker instead directs viewers to connect MetaMask to Remix and send funds to the contract they created. On this record, the identifiable transaction can be read as capital for a speculative trading operation, not necessarily a payment to someone selling a guaranteed payout.

citations.quote: 90% of the profit is sent back to your wallet, and 10% is kept in the Frontrun Pool for the next transaction.
Make sure that your wallet is connected to Remix
we're just going to send some funds to that contract we just created
It automatically buys and sells for you

rebuttal.rebuttal: The opening treats the requested deposit and promised return as decisive. Yet its quoted deployment sequence establishes only that a contract is created and then funded; it does not establish who ultimately receives the funds or what the code actually does. The speaker describes the supposed 90-percent return as going to the viewer's wallet. That account may deserve skepticism, but the cited steps alone do not demonstrate a diverted payment.

citations.quote: we're just going to send some funds to that contract we just created
It will transit it back in your wallet and the remaining 10% will stay in the front running code.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: A credential request or visible diversion is not necessary to identify the concern here. The speaker instructs viewers to put BNB into contract code supplied through the description, asserts that it will trade automatically, and claims large returns. The claim that profits go back to the wallet is part of the pitch, not evidence that the contract does so. The cited material shows the solicitation and its promised payoff, but does not verify the mechanism.
